activities.prompt:
Explain to a friend why print("3" + "4") shows 34 in Python, while print(3 + "4") stops with an error. Show how a conversion can make the mixed-type expression work.

Input requirement: keyboard text entry for the explanation. Read the supplied model and self-check; prose is not automatically graded. A remote alone is insufficient.
activities.explanation:
"3" and "4" are both strings, so + joins them into "34". In 3 + "4", one side is a number and the other a string. Python refuses to guess, so it raises a TypeError. Convert with int("4") to add numbers or str(3) to join strings.

Self-check:
- Quotes make a string; without quotes 3 is a number.
- + joins two strings but adds two numbers.
- Python will not mix a number and a string with +; convert with int() or str().

activities.explanation:
Python treats False, zero, empty strings, empty collections and None as falsy, so if 0: skips. A valid score of 0 needs an explicit test such as score is not None. and / or return operands: 3 or 0 gives 3; 0 and 5 gives 0; None or "guest" gives "guest". An if checks the truthiness of the returned value.

Self-check:
- if tests truthiness, so 0 skips the block even when it is a valid score.
- In Python 0, 0.0, "", empty lists/dicts and None are all falsy.
- Write the comparison you mean (if count > 0, if name != "") when the difference matters.
- and / or return operands, not necessarily bools: 3 or 0 is 3; 0 and 5 is 0; any falsy name makes name or "guest" return "guest".

activities.prompt:
Explain to a friend: what is a base case, what happens without one (or if calls never reach it), and how the call stack lets fact(3) work out 3 × 2 × 1 when no single call knows the whole answer.

Input requirement: keyboard text entry for the explanation. Read the supplied model and self-check; prose is not automatically graded. A remote alone is insufficient.
activities.explanation:
A base case is the smallest version of the problem, answered directly (fact(1) is 1). Without one, or if each call doesn't get closer to it, the function keeps calling itself until Python runs out of stack and raises a RecursionError. fact(3) can't finish until fact(2) does, which waits on fact(1). Each waiting call keeps its own n in its own box on the call stack. fact(1) answers 1, then fact(2) finishes 2 × 1, then fact(3) finishes 3 × 2. The newest box always finishes first.

Self-check:
- The base case answers directly, without calling itself again.
- Every recursive call must move closer to the base case, or calls pile up until RecursionError.
- Each waiting call keeps its own n on the stack; results come back last-in, first-out and combine on the way out.
